content.introduction: The Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged in its final decision before the US midterm elections, according to BBC News. The central bank raised rates for the first time in three years last month to 3.75%-4%, aiming to curb inflation. The decision is anticipated at 14:00 EDT (18:00 GMT). The sources do not provide information on whether the rates will be raised, lowered, or kept unchanged beyond this expectation.
body:
This will be an extremely closely watched meeting from the Federal Reserve. We are less than a week out from the midterm elections, which are being fought around the country over cost of living issues.

Inflation remains higher than the central bank would like. Last month, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time in three years. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the board decided to move because "inflation is too high and has been for too long”. [...] # US central bank to make final interest rate decision before midterm elections

Kevin Warsh

## Summary

The US central bank is expected to leave interest rates unchanged, in the final decision before the US midterm elections - we'll hear the decision at 14:00 EDT (18:00 GMT)

The Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in three years last month to 3.75%-4%. It hinted at additional hikes later this year in an effort to curb inflation [...] The Federal Reserve has been trying to curb inflation - and interest rates, which affect everything from loans to returns on savings, are its main tool for doing so.

For many Americans, cost of living is at the top of their minds as they prepare to vote for their representatives next week. Households are feeling the pinch of rising prices at the petrol pump and in the supermarket.

We'll bring you all the details of the decision here.

The US central bank has cut interest rates by more than expected in its first reduction in over four years.

The Federal Reserve said it would lower the target for its key lending rate by 0.5 percentage points, to the range of 4.75%-5%. [...] The widely expected cut is bigger than many analysts had predicted just a week ago, and comes as officials have noted increasing concern about rising unemployment rates.
